v0.9.0 got fufu invoked. This one is about fufu being usable by somebody who did not write it: a documentation site to send a newcomer to, a policy that steers an agent back to `ff` without ever rewriting its command line, and commit signing, without which a repository carrying a branch-protection rule could not use fufu at all.

**A site to send people to**

Everything fufu knew about itself lived in DESIGN.md, a README walkthrough, and forty-nine `--help` pages. None of that is a document a person reads front to back, and none of it answers "what is this and should I use it" for a reader who has not already decided.

[The site](https://tyler-johnson.github.io/fufu/) is thirty-two hand-written pages organized jj's way — getting started, concepts, guides, reference, comparisons, internals — plus a section jj has no need for: for agents. The first-visit path runs pitch → install → tutorial → adopting → vs-git and vs-jj without hitting a stub. The concepts spine is DESIGN.md rewritten as description rather than argument. Five guides cover recovery, rewriting history, stacked changes, worktrees, and working with plain-git teammates. The agents section runs argument to wiring to wire format: why an agent should be behind fufu, a setup page paste-ready from this repository's own configuration, and a machine-surface specification.

Every console block on the site, and every JSON transcript in that specification, came from a script under `scripts/docs/` run against the built binary in a throwaway repository, so regenerating a page is one invocation when a verb's output changes. That harness is also what corrected the pages: writing the guides surfaced two display bugs, both fixed below.

Two parts of the site generate themselves. The forty-nine help pages moved out of `help.rs` into markdown files under `crates/ff-cli/src/help/`, one unwrapped line per paragraph, rendered to seventy-two columns for the terminal on every invocation. Markdown being the source is what lets `docs/reference/cli/` be fifty-one pages emitted from those same files, under a byte-equality test that fails CI the moment the reference drifts from `--help`; the config key registry is generated the same way. `ff --help` also stopped being forty commands in one alphabetically arbitrary block: the root page groups them under `git help`'s own headings, and `ff -h` shows fourteen common verbs, git's `help` against `help -a` split.

**`fufu.gitPolicy`: correction, never translation**

`fufu.translate` was a boolean, off by default, that made `ff git commit` quietly run `ff commit` instead. It was doing nothing for anybody, and it answered the wrong question — what makes an agent reach for `ff` instead of `git` is not served by silently swapping one write command for another. That is the one thing a correction mechanism must not do, so the execution path is deleted rather than re-gated.

Three tiers replace it in the registry in place, so the setting count stays twelve. `observe` records and says nothing. `coach`, the default, names the fufu alternative the first time a git word comes up. `strict` refuses the words fufu has verbs for and says what to run instead. Both entry points obey one setting: `ff git`, which is what a person types through the recommended alias, and a raw `git …` inside an agent's Bash tool, which `PreToolUse` sees — injected as context under coach, denied with the same text under strict.

Three rules keep it safe. fufu never runs a write verb you did not type. Only the eighteen git words fufu has an answer for are ever touched, so `git apply`, `git bisect`, `git submodule` and `git gc` pass through untouched and `ff git <args…>` stays an honest escape hatch even under strict. And ambiguity fails open: anything that is not one plain `git <word> …` invocation is never coached and never denied. `ff doctor` grows a row reading the tally, silent when nothing has been counted, and the trigger contract's never-vetoes clause is amended where it sat: a hook never vetoes on its own judgment, and vetoes only where config said to.

Alongside it, the briefing reaches every audience. A subagent inherits its parent's session id and fires no prompt event, so under a marker holding one session per client it worked with no idea fufu was there. The marker now records which audiences were briefed inside a session, and a tool call briefs whoever is making it — which is also what reaches a repository the agent has just `cd`'d into. `SessionStart` becomes its own event kind, so a resume, a `/clear` or a compaction re-briefs into the context it just dropped. Claude Code's plugin also gains `Stop` and `SubagentStop` as pure capture: snapshotting happens before an action, so the file state an agent wrote as the last thing in a turn sat uncaptured until whatever came next.

**Commit signing**

fufu writes commit objects itself and gitoxide implements no signing, so `commit.gpgsign` was read nowhere. `ff commit` minted unsigned commits whatever git config said, and every rewrite verb stripped the signature it found with nothing to put back. A repository with a branch-protection rule could not use fufu.

fufu now reads git's keys in git's spelling — `commit.gpgsign`, `gpg.format`, `user.signingkey` and the program keys, plus the ssh allowed-signers, revocation and trust-level keys for verification — and signs in all three formats git signs in: openpgp through gpg, x509 through gpgsm, ssh through ssh-keygen. Nothing was added to the `fufu.*` registry. The signer resolves once per verb above every write, and one that refuses aborts before the journal append and before any ref moves.

`commit.gpgsign` governs replays too, a deliberate departure from git: `git rebase` needs `rebase.gpgSign` said separately and quietly unsigns a branch without it, and a restack that unsigned three commits is the failure this feature exists to prevent. `ff commit` gains `-S` and `--no-sign` for the one-off, and rewrite verbs take the setting, with git's own `GIT_CONFIG_*` escape hatch for overriding one invocation. Op-journal and park commits stay unsigned: the first carries fufu's identity rather than yours, the second never leaves the repository.

Reading signatures back is split by what it costs. Whether a commit carries a signature is a header on an object the log walk already decoded, so `ff log` and `ff status` mark it `signed` by default having spawned nothing; the word is `signed` rather than `verified` because nothing was checked to print it. Whether that signature is good is a signer spawn apiece, so `ff log --signatures` buys the check and says `verified gpg 9B295D68`, or `bad signature`, `untrusted key`, `expired key`, `revoked key`, `unverifiable`. Those checks run in parallel, one per core up to eight: twenty ssh-signed commits go from 245ms to 94ms on four cores. Signing stays sequential, because racing pinentry prompts for one terminal is not a speed-up. `ff show` verifies the one commit it prints, and `ff doctor` has a spawn-free `signing` row that reports whether the setup will work without running anything.

One accepted regression: with signing on, the `@` row shows no predicted sha, because the signature is not knowable without running the signer.

**Two bugs the guides found**

`ff trim` called a live branch gone. A pointer is deleted either because the branch no longer exists or because every operation behind it aged out of the keep window, and one wording served both; the report now records whether `refs/heads/<branch>` resolves, and a live branch is told its operations aged out and it was not touched.

And with two worktrees, park and resume churn in one tree made the other print `refs/heads/<branch> deleted` while the branch lived, then `created at` when it was released — a transition nothing performed, written into the log as a foreign operation. Refs another worktree holds are dropped from observation on purpose, so the stored table was filtered as of when it was written while the observation is filtered as of now. The table now carries held-elsewhere entries forward at their last-known sha. No migration, and the delete direction is fixed immediately even against an old baseline.

**Smaller things**

Three files that had grown past comfort became directory modules with no logic changed: the core's `rewrite.rs` into replay, chain and markers; the CLI's `render.rs` into palette, age, status, diff and rows; and `doctor.rs`, whose 628-line `run()` is now orchestration over checks grouped by the data they share. The docs site deploys itself on a push to main, and a docs-only push no longer spins the rust matrix.

**Numbers**

28 commits over v0.9.0, +17,889/−6,524 across 228 files. 83 pages on the docs site, 51 of them generated. 115 `ff explain` ids, up from 110. 12 config keys, unchanged.
